title: Usage Health Scoring Methodology
text:
The account health score (0-100) blends four weighted signals. Adoption breadth (35%): share of licensed seats active in the trailing 28 days. Engagement depth (25%): frequency and recency of logins and core-feature usage. Relationship strength (20%): presence of an executive sponsor and an active champion. Support and reliability (20%): open high-severity tickets, recent incidents, and CSAT.

A month-over-month decline in weekly active users greater than 20% is a leading churn indicator and should trigger a health-drop review. Loss of a champion with no identified replacement reduces relationship strength materially. Scores below 50 are high risk; below 40 are critical and warrant immediate intervention.

title: Churn Save Playbook Overview
text:
A churn save begins with diagnosis: identify whether risk is driven by product value, relationship, reliability, or commercials, because the remedy differs for each. Value and adoption gaps call for re-onboarding and use-case expansion. Relationship gaps call for re-establishing an executive sponsor. Reliability incidents call for an escalation response with a written RCA. Commercial risk calls for ROI framing before any discount.

Always quantify what is at stake (ARR at risk, renewal date) and pair every save motion with a measurable success metric, for example restoring weekly active users to baseline within 30 days, or moving the health score above 50 before renewal.

title: Product-Qualified Lead (PQL) Expansion Criteria
text:
An account is a product-qualified expansion lead when it shows organic pull, not seller push. Core criteria: seat utilization at or above 90% of licensed seats; additional teams piloting or borrowing logins; a feature request that maps to a higher tier (for example SSO/SCIM or data residency); an economic buyer with NPS 8 or higher; and confirmed budget for the current fiscal year.

When these signals co-occur, lead with a seat-expansion proposal that bundles the enterprise capability they requested and offer a volume-pricing tier. PQL expansions close faster and retain better than cold upsells because value is already proven.

title: Health Drop Recovery Play
text:
Trigger: Weekly active users down more than 20% month over month, or health score falling below 50.
Goal: Restore usage to baseline within 30 days and stabilize the relationship.
Steps: 1) Diagnose the drop, separating product breakage from disengagement. 2) Fix any blocking integration or technical issue with an expedited engineering ticket. 3) Identify and secure a new executive sponsor if the champion has left. 4) Run a targeted re-activation: outreach to dormant users and a refresher on the broken workflow. 5) Set a 30-day usage recovery target and review weekly.
Success metric: WAU back to within 10% of prior baseline and health score above 50 before renewal.

title: Renewal Risk Mitigation Play
text:
Trigger: Renewal within 90 days combined with a competitive evaluation, price pressure, or a weak executive relationship.
Goal: Secure the renewal while protecting ARR.
Steps: 1) Build an ROI summary quantifying delivered value (downtime reduced, throughput or revenue gained). 2) Re-establish the executive relationship with a business review before any pricing conversation. 3) Counter discount requests with a multi-year structure or value-add bundle rather than a flat cut. 4) Address the competitive threat with a differentiation one-pager. 5) Confirm the mutual close plan and signatures timeline.
Success metric: Renewal signed at or above target ARR; discount, if any, exchanged for term length or expansion.

title: Onboarding Acceleration Play
text:
Trigger: Onboarding behind milestone plan (for example fewer than 5 of 7 milestones by day 45), low seat provisioning, or training no-shows.
Goal: Reach first value fast and provision the purchased seats.
Steps: 1) Assign a dedicated implementation specialist to take SSO setup and data import off the customer's plate. 2) Run a focused 2-week milestone sprint targeting the highest-value workflow first. 3) Offer asynchronous, recorded training to fit constrained schedules. 4) Secure a short sponsor checkpoint to confirm priorities and unblock access. 5) Track provisioned-seat count and milestone completion weekly.
Success metric: First value delivered and at least 80% of seats provisioned within 30 days of the rescue.

title: Executive Escalation Response Play
text:
Trigger: Sev-1 incident, repeated outages, or a formal executive escalation, especially near a renewal.
Goal: Contain trust damage and prevent churn.
Steps: 1) Acknowledge same day with a senior leader (VP or above) reaching out directly. 2) Deliver a written root-cause analysis within 48 hours. 3) Provide a concrete remediation roadmap with owners and dates. 4) Proactively offer SLA credits before the customer has to ask. 5) Establish a weekly executive check-in until trust is demonstrably restored.
Success metric: Escalation formally closed, CSAT recovered to 4+ of 5, and renewal retained.

title: Expansion and Upsell Qualification Play
text:
Trigger: Product-qualified expansion signals, seat utilization at or above 90%, additional teams piloting, a tier-mapped feature request, and approved budget.
Goal: Convert organic demand into a clean seat and tier expansion.
Steps: 1) Quantify the pull, naming the teams and the borrowed-login behavior. 2) Build a seat-expansion proposal bundling the requested enterprise capability (for example SSO/SCIM). 3) Offer a volume-pricing tier to reward the larger commitment. 4) Confirm the economic buyer and budget timeline. 5) Tie expansion to a value milestone and a reference or case-study ask.
Success metric: Expansion closed within the current fiscal quarter at or above the proposed seat count.

title: Champion Departure and Sponsor Mapping
text:
Losing a champion is one of the strongest leading indicators of churn because it removes the internal force that drives adoption and defends the renewal. When a champion or executive sponsor leaves, relationship strength in the health score drops immediately and should trigger a sponsor-mapping motion within 14 days.

Steps: 1) Confirm the departure and any interim owner. 2) Map remaining stakeholders by influence and disposition (advocate, neutral, blocker). 3) Identify the most likely new champion based on who derives daily value. 4) Run a value-recap session to convert that person, giving them an internal win to own. 5) Re-establish an executive sponsor before any renewal conversation. Never let an account with a vacant sponsor seat enter a renewal window without a named replacement.

title: Reading Conflicting Signals and When to Hold
text:
Not every dip warrants intervention. Signals conflict when, for example, usage is healthy but an exec is skeptical (relationship risk), or sentiment is negative but tied to a single resolved incident. The planner should separate supporting from contradicting evidence and weigh recency and source reliability.

Prefer a monitor-and-hold posture when: signals are weak or contradictory; a credible remediation is already in flight; or the cost and relationship risk of acting outweighs the expected benefit. When holding, set explicit re-evaluation thresholds (for example, escalate if WAU falls another 10% or if a second incident occurs within 30 days) so the watch list is actionable rather than passive. Holding is a legitimate next best action, not the absence of one.

title: Concession and Discount Guardrails
text:
Concessions protect revenue only when they buy something durable. Never lead a renewal with a discount; lead with value and relationship. A retention concession is appropriate only after a value-realignment attempt and, for at-risk renewals, with leadership approval.

Guardrails: exchange any discount for term length (multi-year), expansion commitment, or a reference, never a flat one-time cut. Cap standard CSM-approved concessions at a defined threshold; anything larger requires CS leadership and finance sign-off. Do not offer a concession to mask a reliability or product problem, fix the underlying issue first. Document the rationale and the quid pro quo so the concession is auditable and repeatable.
